name: Apollonides
bio: Apollonides is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 1st century AD.
This archive carries the 3 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the first volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Books I–VI) (Book VI: 105, 238, 239).

poems.title: Book VI, 105
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text: I, Menis the net-fisher, give to thee, Artemis of the harbour, a grilled red-mullet and a hake, a cup of wine filled to the brim with a piece of dry bread broken into it, a poor sacrifice, in return for which grant that my nets may be always full of fish; for all nets, gracious goddess, are given to thy keeping.

poems.title: Book VI, 238
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text: I, old Euphron, farm no many-furrowed plain or vineyard rich in wine, but I plough a little shallow soil just scraped by the share, and I get but the juice that flows from a few grapes. From my little my gift can be but little, but if, kind god, thou givest me more, thou shalt have the first fruits of my plenty likewise.

poems.title: Book VI, 239
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text: Old Cliton, the bee-keeper, cut me out, the sweet harvest of his swarm, and instead of a victim from the herd offers me, pressing much honey from the ambrosial combs of the spring, the gift of his unshepherded far-flying flock. But make his swarm-bearing company innumerable and fill full the wax-built cells with sweetest nectar.

poems.title: Book VII, 180
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text: The doom of death hath been transferred, and in thy place, master, I, thy slave, fill the loathly grave. When I was building thy tearful chamber underground to lay thy body in after death, the earth around slid and covered me. Hades is not grievous to ne. I shall dwell under thy sun.

poems.title: Book VII, 233
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text: Aquius, the Roman captain, whose armed neck was loaded with golden torques, when he fell into his last illness and saw the end was inevitable, was minded of his own valour and driving his sword into his vitals, said as he was dying “I am vanquished of my own will, lest Disease boast of the deed.”

poems.title: Book VII, 378
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text: Heliodorus went first, and in even less than an hour his wife, Diogenia, followed her dear husband. Both, even as they dwelt together, are interred under one stone, happy to share one tomb, as erst to share one chamber.

poems.title: Book VII, 389
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text: Who is there that has not suffered the extremity of woe, weeping fora son? But the house of Posidippus buried all four, taken from him in four days by death, that cut short all his hopes of them. The father’s mourning eyes drenched with tears have lost their sight, and one may say that a common night now holds them all.

poems.title: Book VII, 631
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text: If thou comest to Apollo’s harbour at Miletus, give to Diogenes the mournful message that his shipwrecked son Diphilus lies in Andrian earth, having drunk the water of the Aegean Sea.

poems.title: Book VII, 642
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text: Between Syrus and Delos the waves engulfed Menoetes of Samos, son of Diaphanes, together with his cargo. For a pious purpose was he hurrying home, but the sea is the enemy even of those who are hastening to be with their fathers in sickness.

poems.title: Book VII, 693
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text: I, the heap of stones by the shore, cover Glenis, who was swept away by the cruel swirl of a wave as he was angling from a steep projecting rock. All his fellow fishermen raised me. Save them, Poseidon, and grant ever to all casters of the line a calm shore.

poems.title: Book VII, 702
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text: The capture of his rod, pulled out of the sea by the six-stranded hair line, was fatal to the fisherman Menestratus; then, when the red phycis, gaping at the errant bait of the murderous hook, swallowed greedily the sharp fraud, as he was cracking its skull with its teeth, it slew him, taking a violent leap and slipping down his throat.”

poems.title: Book VII, 742: Not Sepulchra!
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text: No longer, 'Timoclea, hast thou lost the light of thy eyes, now thou hast given birth to twin boys, but thou art now more perfect than thou ever wast, looking with more than two eyes on the burning Chariot of the Sun.

poems.title: Book IX, 228
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text: Menitea received the unlooked for news that her son, with his cargo, had been engulfed in the waves, and seeing the symbol of her own misfortune in the corpse of another which the sea had washed up on the beach, the unhappy woman gave it burial as if it were her son’s. But Dion, his ship undamaged, returned in safety from a voyage that had met all his hopes. What diverse fortune befel the two mothers! The one holds alive the son she never hoped to see, the other shall not even see her son dead.

poems.title: Book IX, 243
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text: The parents of Aristippus both rejoiced and wept for their son, and one day saw both his good and evil fate. When he had escaped from the burning house, straightway Zeus launched at his head the all-powerful flame of his thunderbolt. Then those who bewailed the dead spoke this word: “Unhappy boy, reserved by Fate for the fire of Heaven!”

poems.title: Book IX, 244
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text: A timid troop of horned deer, when the frozen mountain tops were covered by the snow clouds, sought refuge, poor creatures, in the river, setting off there in the hope of warming their swift limbs in the moist exhalations of the stream. But the unkind stream, shutting them in all of a sudden, imprisoned them in odious fetters of wintry ice. A crowd of countrymen feasted on the unsnared game that had often escaped the net and its stakes,

poems.title: Book IX, 257
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text: ‘I, the Pure Fountain (for that is the name the Nymphs bestowed on me above all other springs), when the robber had slain the men who were reclining beside me, and washed his bloody hands in my sacred water, turned back that sweet stream, and no longer gush for travellers; for who will call me “The Pure” any longer?

poems.title: Book IX, 264
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text: The cicada used to sit on the highest boughs of the shrubs, and in the burning noon-tide sun, beating its belly with its wings, by the sweet variations of its self-wrought strains filled all the wilderness with music. But Criton of Pialia, the fowler who disdains no kind of game, caught this fleshless thing by its back with his limed twig. But he suffered punishment; for his daily craft now plays him false, and he wanders about not catching even a feather.

poems.title: Book IX, 265
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text: The bird of Zeus, pierced by an arrow, avenged himself on the Cretan for his archery, returning arrow for arrow from heaven. With the returning shaft it slew the slayer at once from the sky, and falling, killed as it died. No longer boast, ye Cretans, of your unerring arrows; let the deadly aim of Zeus, too, be celebrated.

poems.title: Book IX, 271
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text: And when then, tell me, Sea, shalt thou give safe passage to ships, if we are to weep even in the days of the halcyons, the haleyons for whom the deep has ever lulled the waves to so steady a calm that they deem it more trustworthy than the land ? Even now, when thou boastest of being a nurse stilling the pangs of child-birth, thou hast sunk Aristomenes with his cargo.

poems.title: Book IX, 280
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text: Laelius the distinguished Roman consul said, looking at the Eurotas, “Hail! Sparta’s stream, of rivers noblest far.” Having thus set his hand to the erudite book of the Muses, he saw over his head a token of learning. The magpies, birds that imitate human life, were calling from the leafy dells in all their various tongues. By them he was encouraged ; and how can the labour not be enviable if even the birds desire (to find expression for their thoughts) ?

poems.title: Book IX, 281
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text: When all Asia witnessed the common marvel the colt furious to feed on flesh of men, the grey-grown legend of the Thracian stable came before my eyes. I am in search of a second Heracles.

poems.title: Book IX, 296
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text: Scyllis, when Xerxes’ huge fleet was driving all Greece before it, invented submarine warfare. Descending into the hidden depths of the realm of Nereus, he cut the cables of the ships’ anchors. The Persian vessels, with all their crews, glided ashore and silently perished —the first achievement of Themistocles.

poems.title: Book IX, 422
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text: “By our children,” she said, “I implore thee, if thou layest me out dead, enter not a second time into the loving bond of wedlock.” She spoke, but he hastened to take another wife. Yet Philinna, even dead, punished Diogenes for forgetting her. For on the first night the wrath from which there is no escape laid their chamber in ruins, so that the sun never shone on his second marriage.

poems.title: Book IX, 791: On a Temple of Aphrodite built in the Sea
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text: Cytherea, who hast established in the depths of the flood the foundations of the sanctuary encinctured by thy mother the sea, around thee the sea rejoices, its blue surface smiling gently under the breeze of Zephyr. Because of this act of piety, and thy temple which Postumus erected, thou shalt boast thee more than because of Paphos.

poems.title: Book IX, 287
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text: I, the holy bird, who had never set foot in Rhodes, the eagle who was but a fable to the people of Cercaphus, came borne through the vast heaven by my high-flying wings, then when Tiberius was in the island of the Sun. In his house I rested, at the beck of my master’s hand, not shrinking from the future Zeus.

poems.title: Book X, 19
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text: Swear on this day, Gaius, the first sweet harvest of thy cheeks and the young curls on thy chin. Thy father Lucius will take in his hand what he had prayed to see, the down of thee who shalt grow to look on many suns. Others give golden presents, but I joyful verses; for indeed the Muse is not the inferior of wealth.

poems.title: Book XI, 25
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text: Thou art asleep, my friend, but the cup itself is calling to thee: ‘“ Awake, and entertain not thyself with this meditation on death.” Spare not, Diodorus, but slipping greedily into wine, drink it unmixed until thy knees give way. The time shall come when we: shall not drink—a long, leng time; but come, haste thee; the age of wisdom is beginning to tint our temples.

poems.title: Book XVI, 49
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text: The olden time admired Cinyras or both the Phrygians, but we, Leo, will sing thy beauty, O renowned son of Cercaphus. Most blessed of islands, then, is Rhodes, on which such a sun shines.

poems.title: Book XVI, 50
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text: If such a Leo (lion) had chanced to face Heracles, this would not have been his twelfth labour.

poems.title: Book XVI, 235: On a Statue of Pan
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text: I am the country-folk’s god. Why do you shed for me offerings from cups of gold, and pour me out strong Italian wine, and bind to the stone the curved necks of bulls? Spare your pains; I take no pleasure in such sacrifices. I, Pan, the dweller on the mountains, carved from a tree-trunk, am a feaster on mutton, and drink my must from a bowl of clay.

poems.title: Book XVI, 239: On the Same
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text: ANaxaGoras set me up here, a Priapus not standing on my feet, but resting both knees on the ground. Phylomachus made me; but seeing lovely Charito standing beside me, you will seek no longer why I fell on my knees.

poems.title: To Artemis of the Fishing-Nets (Mackail)
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: A red mullet and a hake from the embers to thee, Artemis of the Haven, I Menis, the caster of nets, offer, and a brimming cup of wine mixed strong, and a broken crust of dry bread, a poor man's sacrifice; in recompence whereof give thou nets ever filled with prey; to thee, O blessed one, all meshes have been given.

poems.title: The Bloody Well (Mackail)
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: I the Clear Fount (for the Nymphs gave this surname to me beyond all other springs) since a robber slew men who were resting beside me and washed his bloodstained hand in my holy waters, have turned that sweet flow backward, and no longer gush out for wayfarers; for who any more will call me the Clear?

poems.title: The Days of the Halcyons (Mackail)
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: And when shall thy swirling passage be free from fear, say, O sea, if even in the days of the halcyons we must weep, of the halcyons for whom Ocean evermore stills his windless wave, that one might think dry land less trustworthy? but even when thou callest thyself a gentle nurse and harmless to women in labour, thou didst drown Aristomenes with his freight.

poems.title: Undivided (Mackail)
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Heliodorus went first, and Diogeneia the wife, not an hour's space after, followed her dear husband; and both, even as they dwelt together, are buried under this slab, rejoicing in their common tomb even as in a bride-chamber.

poems.title: The Passing of Youth (Mackail)
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Thou slumberest, O comrade; but the cup itself cries to thee, "Awake; do not make thy pleasure in the rehearsal of death." Spare not, Diodorus, slipping greedily into wine, drink deep, even to the tottering of the knee. Time shall be when we shall not drink, long and long; nay come, make haste; prudence already lays her hand on our temples.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.105: Τρῖγλαν ἀπʼ ἀνθρακιῆς καὶ φυκίδα σοί,
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text:
Τρῖγλαν ἀπʼ ἀνθρακιῆς καὶ φυκίδα σοί, λιμενῖτι
Ἄρτεμι, δωρεῦμαι Μῆνις ὁ δικτυβόλος,
καὶ ζωρόν, κεράσας ἰσοχειλέα, καὶ τρύφος ἄρτου,
αὖον ἐπιθραύσας, τὴν πενιχρὴν θυσίην
ἀνθʼ ἧς μοι πλησθέντα δίδου θηράμασιν αἰὲν
δίκτυα· σοὶ δέδοται πάντα, μάκαιρα, λίνα.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.238: εὔφρων οὐ πεδίου πολυαύλακός εἰμʼ ὁ
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text:
εὔφρων οὐ πεδίου πολυαύλακός εἰμʼ ὁ γεραιὸς
οὐδὲ πολυγλεύκου γειομόρος βότρυος·
ἀλλʼ ἀρότρῳ βραχύβωλον ἐπικνίζοντι χαράσσω
χέρσον, καὶ βαιοῦ πίδακα ῥαγὸς ἔχω.
εἴη δʼ ἐξ ὀλίγων ὀλίγη χάρις· εἰ δὲ διδοίης
πλείονα, καὶ πολλῶν, δαῖμον, ἀπαρξόμεθα,

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.239: Σμήνεος ἔκ με ταμὼν γλυκερὸν θέρος
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text:
Σμήνεος ἔκ με ταμὼν γλυκερὸν θέρος ἀντὶ νομαίων
γηραιὸς Κλείτων σπεῖσε μελισσοπόνος,
ἀμβροσίων ἔαρος κηρῶν μέλι πολλὸν ἀμέλξας,
δῶρον ἀποιμάντου τηλεπέτευς ἀγέλης.
θείης δʼ ἑσμοτόκον χορὸν ἄπλετον, εὖ δὲ μελιχροῦ
νέκταρος ἐμπλήσαις κηροπαγεῖς θαλάμας.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.180: ἠλλάχθη θανάτοιο τεὸς μόρος, ἀντὶ δὲ
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text:
ἠλλάχθη θανάτοιο τεὸς μόρος, ἀντὶ δὲ σεῖο,
δέσποτα, δοῦλος ἐγὼ στυγνὸν ἔπλησα τάφον
ἡνίκα σεῦ δακρυτὰ κατὰ χθονὸς ἠρία τεῦχον,
ὡς ἂν ἀποφθιμένου κεῖθι δέμας κτερίσω·
ἀμφὶς ˘ ἔμʼ ὤλισθεν γυρὴ κόνις. οὐ βαρὺς ἡμῖν
ἔστʼ Ἀίδης· ζήσω τὸν σὸν ὑπʼ ἠέλιον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.233: Αἴλιος, Αὐσονίης στρατιῆς πρόμος, ὁ χρυσέοισι
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text:
Αἴλιος, Αὐσονίης στρατιῆς πρόμος, ὁ χρυσέοισι
στέμμασι σωρεύσας αὐχένας ὁπλοφόρους,
νοῦσον ὅτʼ εἰς ὑπάτην ὠλίσθανε τέρμα τʼ ἄφυκτον
εἶδεν, ἀριστείην † ἐμφανὲς εἰς ἰδίην
πῆξε δʼ ὑπὸ σπλάγχνοισιν ἑὸν ξίφος, εἶπέ τε θνῄσκων
αὐτὸς ἑκὼν ἐδάμην, μὴ νόσος εὖχος ἔχῃ.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.378: ἔφθανεν Ἡλιόδωρος, ἐφέσπετο δʼ, οὐδʼ ὅσον
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text:
ἔφθανεν Ἡλιόδωρος, ἐφέσπετο δʼ, οὐδʼ ὅσον ὥρῃ
ὕστερον, ἀνδρὶ φίλῳ Διογένεια δάμαρ.
ἄμφω δʼ, ὡς ἅμʼ ἔναιον, ὑπὸ πλακὶ τυμβεύονται,
ξυνὸν ἀγαλλόμενοι καὶ τάφον ὡς θάλαμον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.389: καὶ τίς ὃς οὐκ ἔτλη κακὸν
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text:
καὶ τίς  ὃς οὐκ ἔτλη κακὸν ἔσχατον υἱέα κλαύσας;
ἀλλʼ ὁ Ποσειδίππου πάντας ἔθαψε δόμος
τέσσαρας, οὓς Ἀίδαο συνήριθμον ἥρπασεν ἦμαρ,
τὴν πολλὴν παίδων ἐλπίδα κειραμένου.
πατρὸς δʼ ὄμματα λυγρὰ κατομβρηθέντα γόοισιν
ὤλετο· κοινή που νὺξ μία πάντας ἔχει.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.631: ἢν ἄρα Μιλήτου Φοιβήιον 〈ὅρμον〉 ἵκησθε,
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text:
ἢν ἄρα Μιλήτου Φοιβήιον 〈ὅρμον〉 ἵκησθε,
λέξατε Διογένει πένθιμον ἀγγελίην,
παῖς ὅτι οἱ ναυηγὸς ὑπὸ χθονὶ κεύθεται Ἄνδρου
Δίφιλος, Αἰγαίου κῦμα πιὼν πελάγευς.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.642: Σύρου καὶ Δήλοιο κλύδων μέσος υἷα
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text:
Σύρου καὶ Δήλοιο κλύδων μέσος υἷα Μενοίτην
σὺν φόρτῳ Σαμίου κρύψε Διαφανέος,
εἰς ὅσιον σπεύδοντα πλόου τάχος· ἀλλὰ θάλασσα
ἐχθρὴ καὶ νούσῳ πατρὸς ἐπειγομένοις.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.693: Γλῆνιν παρῃονῖτις ἀμφέχω χερμάς,
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text:
Γλῆνιν παρῃονῖτις ἀμφέχω χερμάς,
πικρῇ κατασπασθέντα κύματος δίνῃ,
ὅτʼ ἰχθυάζετʼ ἐξ ἄκρης ἀπορρῶγος·
χῶσαν δὲ μʼ ὅσσος λαὸς ἦν συνεργήτης,
Πόσειδον, οὓς σὺ σῷζε, καὶ γαληναίην
αἰὲν διδοίης ὁρμιηβόλοις θῖνα.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.702: Ἰχθυοθηρητῆρα Μενέστρατον ὤλεσεν ἄγρη
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text:
Ἰχθυοθηρητῆρα Μενέστρατον ὤλεσεν ἄγρη
δούνακος, ἑξαμίτης ἐκ τριχὸς ἑλκομένη,
εἶδαρ ὅτʼ ἀγκίστρου φόνιον πλάνον ἀμφιχανοῦσα
ὀξείην ἐρυθρὴ φυκὶς ἔβρυξε πάγην·
ἀγνυμένη δʼ ὑπʼ ὀδόντι κατέκτανεν, ἅλματι λάβρῳ
ἐντὸς ὀλισθηρῶν δυσαμένη φαρύγων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.742: οὐκέτι Τιμόκλεια τεῶν φάος ὤλεσας ὄσσων
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text:
οὐκέτι Τιμόκλεια τεῶν φάος ὤλεσας ὄσσων
κούρους δοιοτόκῳ νηδύι γειναμένη·
ὄμμασι δʼ ἐν πλεόνεσσιν ἀθρεῖς πυριθαλπὲς ʽὄχημα
ἠελίου, προτέρης οὖσα τελειοτέρη.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.228: ἀγγελίης ἤκουσεν ἀνωΐστου Μελίτεια,
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text:
ἀγγελίης ἤκουσεν ἀνωΐστου Μελίτεια,
υἱέα σὺν φόρτῳ κύματι κρυπτόμενον·
ἠιόσιν δʼ ἐπικέλσαν ἁλίκλυστον δέμας ἄλλου
δύσμορος οἰκείης σύμβολον εἶδε τύχης,
υἱέα δʼ ὣς ἔστειλε. Δίων δʼ ἐπὶ νηὸς ἀθραύστου
ἤλυθεν εὐκταίης σῶος ἀπʼ ἐμπορίης.
μητέρες ὡς ἀνίσου μοίρης λάχον ἡ μὲν ἄελπτον
ζωὸν ἔχει, κείνη δʼ ὄψεται οὐδὲ νέκυν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.243: γήθησαν περὶ παιδὸς Ἀριστίπποιο τοκῆες,
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text:
γήθησαν περὶ παιδὸς Ἀριστίπποιο τοκῆες,
καὶ κλαῦσαν μοίρης δʼ ἦμαρ ἓν ἀμφοτέρης.
εὖτε γὰρ αἰθόμενον δόμον ἔκφυγεν, ἰθὺ κεραυνοῦ
Ζεὺς κατὰ οἱ κεφαλῆς ἄσπετον ἧκε σέλας.
τοῦτο δʼ ἔπος τότʼ ἔλεξαν ὅσοι νέκυν ὠδύροντο·
ὦ πυρὶ δαιμονίῳ τλῆμον ὀφειλόμενε.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.244: Δειματόεις ἐλάφων κεραὸς λόχος, εὖτε κρυώδεις
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text:
Δειματόεις ἐλάφων κεραὸς λόχος, εὖτε κρυώδεις
πλῆσαν ὀρῶν κορυφὰς χιόνεαι νιφάδες,
δείλαιαι ποταμοῖσιν ἐφώρμισαν, ἐλπίδι φροῦδοι
χλιῆναι νοτεροῖς ἄσθμασιν ὠκὺ γόνυ.
τὰς δὲ περιφράξας ἐχθρὸς ῥόος ἀθρόον ἄφνω
χειμερίῃ στυγεροῦ δῆσε πάγοιο πέδῃ.
πληθὺς δʼ ἀγροτέρων ἀλίνου θοινήσατο θήρης,
ἣ φύγεν ἁρπεδόνην πολλάκι καὶ στάλικα.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.257: ἡ Καθαρὴ ʽ Νύμφαι γὰρ ἐπώνυμον
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text:
ἡ Καθαρὴ ʽ Νύμφαι γὰρ ἐπώνυμον ἔξοχον ἄλλων
κρήνῃ πασάων δῶκαν ἐμοὶ λιβάδωνʼ,
ληιστὴς ὅτε μοι παρακλίντορας ἔκτανεν ἄνδρας,
καὶ φονίην ἱεροῖς ὕδασι λοῦσε χέρα,
κεῖνον ἀναστρέψασα γλυκὺν ῥόον, οὐκέθʼ ὁδίταις
βλύζω· τίς  γὰρ ἐρεῖ τὴν Καθαρὴν ἔτι με;

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.271: καὶ πότε δὴ νήεσσ’ ἄφοβος πόρος,
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text:
καὶ πότε δὴ νήεσσ’ ἄφοβος πόρος, εἰπέ, θάλασσα,
εἰ καὶ ἐν ἀλκυόνων ἤμασι κλαυσόμεθα,
ἀλκυόνων, αἷς πόντος ἀεὶ στηρίξατο κῦμα
νήνεμον, ὡς κρῖναι χέρσον ἀπιστοτέρην;
ἀλλὰ καὶ ἡνίκα μαῖα καὶ ὠδίνεσσιν ἀπήμων
αὐχεῖς, σὸν φόρτῳ δῦσας Ἀριστομένην.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.280: Λαίλιος, Αὐσονίων ὑπάτων κλέος, εἶπεν ἀθρήσας
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text:
Λαίλιος, Αὐσονίων ὑπάτων κλέος, εἶπεν ἀθρήσας
Εὐρώταν· Σπάρτης χαῖρε φέριστον ὕδωρ.
Μουσάων δʼ ἐπὶ χεῖρα βαλὼν πολυΐστορι βίβλῳ,
εἶδεν ὑπὲρ κορυφῆς σύμβολον εὐμαθίης·
κίτται, μιμηλὸν βιότου πτερόν, ἐν σκιεροῖσιν
ἄγκεσι παμφώνων μέλπον ἀπὸ στομάτων.
ὡρμήθη δʼ ἐπὶ ταῖσι. τί δʼ οὐ ζηλωτὸς ὁ μόχθος,
εἰ καὶ πτηνὰ ποθεῖ

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.281: ξυνὸν ὁπηνίκα θαῦμα κατείδομεν Ἀσὶς ἅπασα,
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text:
ξυνὸν ὁπηνίκα θαῦμα κατείδομεν Ἀσὶς ἅπασα,
πῶλον ἐπʼ ἀνδρομέαν σάρκα φριμασσόμενον,
Θρηικίης φάτνης πολιὸς λόγος εἰς ἐμὸν ὄμμα
ἤλυθε δίζημαι δεύτερον Ἡρακλέα.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.287: ὁ πρὶν ἐγὼ Ῥοδίοισιν ἀνέμβατος ἱερὸς
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text:
ὁ πρὶν ἐγὼ Ῥοδίοισιν ἀνέμβατος ἱερὸς ὄρνις,
ὁ πρὶν Κερκαφίδαις αἰετὸς ἱστορίη,
ὑψιπετῆ τότε ταρσὸν ἀνὰ πλατὺν ἠέρʼ ἀερθεὶς
ἤλυθον, Ἠελίου νῆσον ὅτʼ εἶχε Νέρων
κείνου δʼ αὐλίσθην ἐνὶ δώμασι, χειρὶ συνήθης
κράντορος, οὐ φεύγων Ζῆνα τὸν ἐσσόμενον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.296: Σκύλλος, ὅτε Ξέρξου δολιχὸς στόλος Ἑλλάδα
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text:
Σκύλλος, ὅτε Ξέρξου δολιχὸς στόλος Ἑλλάδα πᾶσαν
ἤλαυνεν, βυθίην εὕρετο ναυμαχίην,
Νηρῆος λαθρίοισιν ὑποπλεύσας τενάγεσσι,
καὶ τὸν ἀπʼ ἀγκύρης ὅρμον ἔκειρε νεῶν.
αὔτανδρος δʼ ἐπὶ γῆν ὠλίσθανε Περσὶς ἄναυδος
ὀλλυμένη, πρώτη πεῖρα Θεμιστοκλέους.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.422: πρὸς παίδων εἶπεν “γουνάζομαι, ἤν με
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text:
πρὸς παίδων εἶπεν “γουνάζομαι, ἤν με θανοῦσαν
στείλῃς, μὴ σπεῖσαι δεύτερα φίλτρα γάμου.”
εἶπεν ὁ δʼ εἰς ἑτέρην ἐσπούδασεν. ἀλλὰ Φίλιννα
Διογένην λήθης τίσατο καὶ φθιμένη·
νυκτὶ γὰρ ἐν πρώτῃ θάλαμον σχάσε μῆνις ἄφυκτος,
ὡς μὴ λέκτρον ἰδεῖν δεύτερον ἠέλιον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.791: μητρὶ περιστεφέος σηκοῦ, Κυθέρεια, θαλάσσῃ
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text:
μητρὶ περιστεφέος σηκοῦ, Κυθέρεια, θαλάσσῃ
κρηπῖδας βυθίας οἴδματι πηξαμένη·
χαίρει δʼ ἀμφὶ σὲ πόντος, ἐπὶ ζεφύροιο πνοῇσιν
ἀφρὸν ὑπὲρ νώτου κυάνεον γελάσας.
εἵνεκα δʼ εὐσεβίης, νηοῦ θʼ ὃν ἐγείρατο σεῖο
Πόστουμος, αὐχήσῃ μέζον, †    αφλοισι Πάφου.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca X.19: ἡδὺ παρειάων πρῶτον θέρος ἤματι τούτῳ
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text:
ἡδὺ παρειάων πρῶτον θέρος ἤματι τούτῳ
κείρεο, καὶ γενύων ἠιθέους ἕλικας,
Γάιε· σὸν δὲ πατὴρ χερὶ δέξεται εὐκτὸν ἴουλον
Λεύκιος, αὐξομένου πουλὺν ἐς ἠέλιον.
δωρεῦνται χρυσέοισιν, ἐγὼ δʼ ἱλαροῖς ἐλέγοισιν
οὐ γὰρ δὴ πλούτου Μοῦσα χερειοτέρη.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.25: Ὑπνώεις, ὦ ʼταῖρε· τὸ δὲ σκύφος
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text:
Ὑπνώεις, ὦ ʼταῖρε· τὸ δὲ σκύφος αὐτὸ,βοᾷ σε·
ἔγρεο, “μὴ τέρπου μοιριδίῃ μελέτῃ.
μὴ” φείσῃ, Διόδωρε· λάβρος δʼ εἰς Βάκχον ὀλισθὼν,
ἄχρις ἐπὶ σφαλεροῦ ζωροπότει γόνατος.
ἔσσεθʼ ὅτʼ οὐ πιόμεσθα, πολὺς πολύς· ἀλλʼ ἄγʼ ἐπείγου·
ἡ συνετὴ κροτάφων ἅπτεται ἡμετέρων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XVI.49: θαύμασε τὸν Κινύρην ὁ πάλαι χρόνος
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text:
θαύμασε τὸν Κινύρην ὁ πάλαι χρόνος ἢ Φρύγας ἄμφω·
σὸν δέ, Λέων, ἡμεῖς κάλλος ἀεισόμεθα,
Κερκαφίδη περίβωτε· μακαρτάτη ἔστʼ ἄρα νήσων
καὶ Ῥόδος, ἣ τοίῳ λάμπεται ἠελίῳ.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XVI.50: εἰ τοιόσδε Λέων λάχεν ἀντίος Ἡρακλῆι,
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text:
εἰ τοιόσδε Λέων λάχεν ἀντίος Ἡρακλῆι,
οὐκ ἦν Ἀλκίδεω τοῦτο τὸ δωδέκατον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XVI.235: ἀγροτέρων θεός εἰμι· τί μοι χρυσέοις
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text:
ἀγροτέρων θεός εἰμι· τί μοι χρυσέοις δεπάεσσι
σπένδετε, τοῦ δʼ Ἰταλοῦ χεῖτε μέθυ Βρομίου,
καὶ γυροὺς ταύρων πέτρῃ προσδεῖτε τένοντας;
φείσασθʼ· οὐ τούτοις θύμασι τερπόμεθα.
Πὰν ὁ παρωρείτης, αὐτόξυλος, ἀρνεοθοίνης
εἰμί, καὶ ἐγχθονίου γλευκοπότης κύλικος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XVI.239: ἄνθετʼ Ἀναξαγόρης με, τὸν οὐκ ἐπὶ
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text:
ἄνθετʼ Ἀναξαγόρης με, τὸν οὐκ  ἐπὶ ποσσὶ Πρίηπον,
ἐν χθονὶ δʼ ἀμφοτέρῳ γούνατι κεκλιμένον·
τεῦξε δὲ Φυλόμαχος. Χαριτὼ δέ μοι ἀγχόθι καλὴν
ἀθρήσας, δίζευ μηκέτι πῶς ἔπεσον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.408: εἴθε με παντοίοισιν ἔτι πλάζεσθαι ἀήταις
poems.author: Apollonides
poems.text:
εἴθε με παντοίοισιν ἔτι πλάζεσθαι ἀήταις
ἢ Λητοῖ στῆναι μαῖαν ἀλωομένῃ·
οὐκ ἂν χητοσύνην τόσον ἔστενον. οἱ ἐμὲ δειλήν,
ὅσσαις Ἑλλήνων νηυσὶ παραπλέομαι,
δῆλος ἐρημαίη, τὸ πάλαι σέβας. ὀψέ πη Ἥρη
Λητοῦς, ἀλλʼ οἰκτρὴν τήνδʼ ἐπέθηκε δίκην.
